topics.title: GOC Standards for Optical Students
topics.summary: The General Optical Council (GOC) regulates optometrists, dispensing opticians and students in training. As a registered student you're expected to meet the GOC's Standards for Optical Students: putting patients first, communicating well, getting consent, working within your competence, being honest, and behaving professionally — in and out of clinic, including online.
keyPoints: Optometry students in the UK must be registered with the GOC while training.
The Standards for Optical Students set out the behaviour expected; they mirror the Standards of Practice for registrants.

Themes include: listening to patients and putting them first, communicating effectively, obtaining valid consent, showing care and respect, protecting confidentiality, working within your competence and under supervision.
Also: being honest and trustworthy, being candid when things go wrong, raising concerns about patient safety, and maintaining public confidence in the profession.
Professional behaviour applies outside clinic too — including social media.
Concerns about a student's fitness to train can be raised with the university and the GOC.
Check optical.org for the current version (new standards came into effect from January 2025).
examTraps: Thinking the standards only apply in clinic.
Forgetting that students must be GOC-registered.
Quoting old wording — always refer to the current version.

diagram.description: A circle labelled 'The patient' in the centre, surrounded by segments: communication, consent, care and respect, confidentiality, competence and supervision, honesty and candour, raising concerns, professionalism (including online).

goDeeper.heading: Working within your competence
goDeeper.body: As a student you work under supervision. Know what you're allowed to do, ask when unsure, never present yourself as qualified, and make sure patients know you're a student. If something is beyond you, stop and get your supervisor — that's professional, not a weakness.

goDeeper.heading: Social media and conduct
goDeeper.body: Don't post about patients (even 'anonymised' stories can identify people), don't share clinic photos with patient information, and think about how posts reflect on the profession. Conduct outside clinic — including academic honesty — counts towards fitness to train.

flashcards.front: Who regulates optometry students in the UK?

flashcards.back: Yes — with the GOC, while training.
Yes — professional behaviour includes social media.

flashcards.front: Where to find the current standards

mcq.q: A classmate posts a funny story about a clinic patient without their name. What's the issue?

options.text: It could still identify the patient, so it's a breach
options.feedback: Yes — details can identify people, and it undermines trust.

options.text: No issue, because no name was used in the post
options.feedback: Other details can still identify someone.

options.text: Only an issue if the patient happens to see it
options.feedback: The breach happens when it's posted.

options.text: None: the GOC standards don't apply to students
options.feedback: They do — there are specific Standards for Optical Students.

mcq.explanation: Confidentiality and professional conduct apply online and offline; 'anonymised' stories can still identify patients.

mcq.q: Must optometry students be registered with the GOC while training?

options.text: Only if they work in practice

mcq.explanation: Optometry students must be on the GOC's student register for the whole of their training, from the start, not just once they qualify.

mcq.q: Do the Standards for Optical Students apply outside clinic?

options.text: No, they only apply inside clinic

mcq.explanation: The student standards cover behaviour everywhere, including social media, because conduct outside clinic can affect public confidence in the profession.

mcq.q: A lecturer is worried that a student's behaviour may make them unsafe with patients. Who can the concern be raised with?
mcq.explanation: Concerns about a student's fitness to train can be raised with the university and the GOC.

original.q: Who can a concern about a student's fitness to train be raised with?

mcq.q: A student starts instilling drops without explaining what they're for. Which theme of the student standards are they failing?
mcq.explanation: The standards include obtaining valid consent, communicating effectively and putting patients first.

original.q: Which is a theme of the student standards?

options.text: Selling as many glasses as possible

mcq.q: A student quotes the GOC student standards from a 2019 handout. What should they do?

options.text: Check optical.org for the current version
Keep using the 2019 handout as it is
options.feedback: It may be out of date.

mcq.explanation: New GOC standards for students came into effect from January 2025; always check the current version.

original.q: When did the new GOC student standards come into effect?

options.feedback: Yes; check optical.org for the current version.

mcq.q: How should you introduce yourself to a patient as a student?

options.text: As a student optometrist, under supervision
As a qualified optometrist, to reassure them
By first name only, without saying your role
You needn't say anything about your role

mcq.explanation: Patients have a right to know who is examining them, so you must say you're a student optometrist working under supervision.

mcq.q: What should you do when something goes wrong in your care?

options.text: Be candid with the patient and your supervisor
Hide it and correct the record later
Blame the patient for not explaining clearly
Wait to see whether the patient notices

mcq.explanation: Being candid means telling the patient and your supervisor straight away when something goes wrong, so it can be put right.

mcq.q: What does 'putting patients first' include?

options.text: Listening to them and involving them in decisions
Deciding everything for them to save time
Keeping every examination as short as possible
Only seeing patients with simple problems

mcq.explanation: Putting patients first means listening to them, respecting their views and involving them in decisions about their care.

mcq.q: Where do the student standards mirror?

options.text: The Standards of Practice for registrants
The NHS pay scales for optical staff

mcq.explanation: The Standards for Optical Students mirror the Standards of Practice for registrants, preparing students for the duties they'll have once qualified.

mcq.q: What's the main risk of posting about clinic on social media?

options.text: None, if the account is set to private
Only that the post might go viral
Mainly that it wastes clinic time

mcq.explanation: Even a private post can be shared, and details of patients or clinic can breach confidentiality or fall below professional standards.

mcq.q: On placement, a student is asked to assess a complex patient alone while the supervisor is out. What should they do?

options.text: Explain they need supervision for this
Go ahead and sign it off themselves
Refuse to see any more patients that day
Guess the findings and check them later

mcq.explanation: Students must work within their competence and under supervision.

original.q: Under the standards, you should work

options.text: within your competence and under supervision

mcq.q: Personal relationships with patients are

options.text: fine, as long as both are over eighteen
encouraged, as it builds patient trust

mcq.explanation: Relationships with patients cross professional boundaries and can harm trust, so they're inappropriate whatever the ages involved.

mcq.q: A patient offers you an expensive gift. What do you do?

options.text: Decline politely or follow the practice policy
Accept it, as refusing would be rude
Ask whether they could give something more
Ignore the offer and say nothing at all

mcq.explanation: Expensive gifts can create a sense of obligation or look like a conflict of interest, so decline politely or follow the practice's policy.

mcq.q: Records must be
mcq.explanation: Records are legal documents other clinicians rely on, so they must be honest, accurate and never altered to look better.

mcq.q: Why offer a chaperone?

options.text: To protect patient dignity and you

mcq.explanation: A chaperone protects the patient's dignity and comfort and also protects you, especially for close examinations or vulnerable patients.

mcq.q: Your personal beliefs should

options.text: not affect the care patients receive

mcq.explanation: Your personal beliefs must not affect the care a patient gets; every patient is entitled to the same standard of care.

mcq.q: What does 'fitness to practise' cover?

options.text: Whether a registrant is safe and fit to work

mcq.explanation: Fitness to practise is about whether a registrant has the skills, knowledge, health and character to practise safely.

mcq.q: Who regulates optometrists in the UK?
mcq.explanation: The General Optical Council (GOC) is the UK regulator for optometrists, dispensing opticians and students. The AOP and College are professional bodies.

mcq.q: Treating patients with dignity includes

options.text: privacy, respect and explaining what you do
rushing to keep the clinic on time
talking over them to a colleague

mcq.explanation: Treating patients with dignity means protecting their privacy, being respectful and explaining what you're doing and why.

mcq.q: Two students discuss a named patient's diagnosis on a crowded bus. What's the problem?

options.text: It's fine if the patient isn't there

mcq.explanation: Discussing a named patient where others can overhear is a breach of confidentiality, whoever is talking.

mcq.q: A student copies a classmate's assignment. Why does the GOC care?

options.text: It raises questions about fitness to train
It doesn't: it's a university matter only
Only the university cares about cheating
Only if the student is caught twice

mcq.explanation: Copying is dishonest, and honesty is central to fitness to train, so the GOC can treat it as a professional matter, not just an academic one.

mcq.q: A student signs a supervisor's name in their logbook. How serious is it?

options.text: Very serious: falsifying records is dishonest
Minor, if the work was really done
Acceptable if the supervisor is busy
Normal practice on a busy placement

mcq.explanation: Signing someone else's name falsifies a record, a serious act of dishonesty that can lead to fitness to train proceedings.

mcq.q: A student receives a police caution. What should they do?

options.text: Declare it to the GOC and the university
Hide it, as a caution isn't a conviction
Tell only close friends about it
Wait until they are fully qualified

mcq.explanation: Students must declare cautions and convictions to the GOC and their university; hiding them is itself a serious breach.

mcq.q: How often do students renew GOC registration?
mcq.explanation: Student registration with the GOC is renewed every year, with declarations about health and character.

mcq.q: A student turns up to clinic after drinking alcohol. What should the supervisor do?

options.text: Stop them seeing patients and follow procedure
Let them carry on if they seem fine
Ignore it, as it's a personal matter
Give them coffee and let them continue

mcq.explanation: Someone affected by alcohol may not be safe with patients, so they must stop seeing patients and the matter be dealt with under procedure.

mcq.q: Can you take a photo of an interesting fundus on your personal phone?

options.text: No: use approved systems with consent
Yes, if you crop the name

mcq.explanation: Patient images are personal data. Use the practice's approved systems with the patient's consent, never your own phone.

mcq.q: A patient discloses that a child at home may be at risk. What do you do?

options.text: Follow safeguarding procedures and report to the lead
Tell the child's school directly without procedure

mcq.explanation: A possible risk to a child must go through safeguarding procedures to the safeguarding lead; don't investigate yourself.

mcq.q: A student is unsure how to do a test on a patient. What should they do?

options.text: Ask the supervisor rather than guess
Guess, then check the result later
Skip the test without saying so

mcq.explanation: You must only work within your competence, so if you're unsure, ask your supervisor rather than guess.

mcq.q: What can the GOC do if a registrant's fitness to practise is impaired?

options.text: Impose conditions, suspend or erase them
Close every practice they work in

mcq.explanation: If fitness to practise is impaired, the GOC can impose conditions, suspend the registrant or erase them from the register.

mcq.q: A university has concerns about a student's repeated lateness to clinic. Who usually deals with this first?

options.text: The university's fitness to train process
The police, as a public order issue
The patients whose clinics were late

mcq.explanation: Universities usually handle fitness to train concerns first, involving the GOC as needed.

original.q: Who usually handles a student's fitness to train concerns first?

options.feedback: Yes, with the GOC involved as needed.

mcq.q: Registered optometrists must have

options.text: a second degree in a science

mcq.explanation: Registrants must have professional indemnity insurance, so patients can be compensated if something goes wrong.

mcq.q: A student's behaviour outside clinic can matter because

options.text: it never matters to the GOC

mcq.explanation: Behaviour outside clinic can affect public confidence in the profession, so it can be relevant to fitness to practise or train.

mcq.q: A patient asks you out after their appointment. What should you do?

options.text: Accept, as the appointment is over
Ignore them at every future visit
Tell everyone in the practice about it

mcq.explanation: Professional boundaries apply even after an appointment, so decline politely and carry on treating them professionally.

mcq.q: What's the right way to dress for clinic?

options.text: However you like, as long as you're clean
Long sleeves and jewellery at all times
In fancy dress to put children at ease

mcq.explanation: Clinic dress should look professional and follow infection control rules, such as being bare below the elbows.

mcq.q: Why shouldn't you use your mobile phone while examining a patient?

options.text: It's fine if the patient doesn't mind
Only if it is switched to silent
It helps you look things up quickly

mcq.explanation: Using your phone during an exam is unprofessional, distracts you, and risks recording or sharing confidential information.

mcq.q: A student realises they forgot to test pupils. What should they do?

options.text: Tell the supervisor and complete the test
Hide it, as the pupils were probably fine
Leave it, as the patient has gone

mcq.explanation: Missing a test must be put right honestly: tell the supervisor and complete it, never write a result you didn't measure.

mcq.q: Cheating in an exam can lead to

options.text: nothing, if it was a first offence
better grades and no other effect

mcq.explanation: Exam cheating is dishonesty, which can lead to fitness to train proceedings as well as academic penalties.

mcq.q: A patient's relative phones to ask about the patient's results. What do you do?

options.text: Don't share without the patient's consent
Share only the bad news, gently

mcq.explanation: Health information is confidential, even from family, so it can only be shared with the patient's consent.

mcq.q: Why must students be honest about their health?

options.text: Some conditions may affect safe practice
So they can be excluded from the course
So the clinic can bill correctly

mcq.explanation: Some health conditions could affect safe practice, so honest declarations let support or adjustments be put in place.

mcq.q: The GOC's main purpose is to
mcq.explanation: The GOC's main purpose is to protect the public by regulating the optical professions.

mcq.q: Which body represents optometrists' interests?
mcq.explanation: The Association of Optometrists (AOP) represents optometrists' interests; the GOC is the regulator, which protects the public.

mcq.q: A student shares exam questions online after a test. What's the issue?

options.text: Nothing, once the exam has finished
Only a problem if they were paid

mcq.explanation: Sharing exam questions breaches academic integrity rules and is dishonest, which can affect fitness to train.

mcq.q: A patient complains about a student's attitude. What's the right response?

options.text: Listen, apologise and involve the supervisor
Argue back to defend the student
Ignore it, as attitude is subjective
Delete the record of the appointment

mcq.explanation: Listen to the complaint, apologise, and involve the supervisor, who is responsible for the patient's care.

mcq.q: Why must you only work within your competence?
mcq.explanation: Working beyond your competence risks harming patients, which is why the standards require it.

mcq.q: A student sees a fellow student acting unsafely with a patient. What should they do?
mcq.explanation: Patient safety comes first, so a concern about unsafe practice should be raised with the supervisor straight away.

mcq.q: What's the risk of 'liking' a patient's social media post?

options.text: None: liking a post means nothing
It improves the care they receive

mcq.explanation: Interacting with patients on social media can blur the boundary between a professional and a personal relationship.

mcq.q: Which is a GOC FtP sanction?

options.text: Free CPD courses for a year
None: the GOC has no sanctions

mcq.explanation: GOC fitness to practise sanctions include conditions, suspension and erasure from the register.

mcq.q: Which is an example of 'showing care and respect'?

options.text: Talking over them to a colleague

mcq.explanation: Showing care and respect means explaining what you're doing and respecting the patient's choices.

mcq.q: Why should you not accept cash tips from patients?

options.text: It may look like a conflict of interest
It's always illegal to accept money
It's fine: tips are a normal perk
Only because of tax on the income

mcq.explanation: Cash from patients can look like it's affecting your care, a possible conflict of interest, so follow your practice's policy.

cases.scenario: A student posts a photograph from clinic on social media. A patient's record card, with their name on it, is readable in the background.
cases.question: Which standards has the student breached and what should they do now?
cases.modelAnswer: The GOC Standards for Optical Students require students to keep patient information confidential and to behave online in a way that maintains public confidence in the profession. This is a breach of confidentiality and a data protection incident, whether or not it was intended. They should delete the post at once, tell their supervisor or tutor straight away, and follow the university and clinic's incident procedure, which may include telling the patient. Being open and reflecting on it matters: concealing it would be a far more serious probity issue.

topics.askClaude: Give me 5 professionalism dilemmas a 2nd-year optometry student might face and ask me what the GOC standards would expect me to do.

topics.title: Communication and consent
topics.summary: Valid consent must be voluntary, informed and given by someone with capacity. Good communication makes consent meaningful: explain what you'll do and why, check understanding, and respect the answer.
keyPoints: Valid consent: voluntary (no pressure), informed (benefits, risks, alternatives), and the person has capacity.
Consent can be verbal, written or implied — but implied consent shouldn't be assumed for anything invasive (e.g. drops, contact tonometry).

Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England & Wales): assume capacity unless shown otherwise; a person lacks capacity for a decision if they can't understand, retain, use/weigh the information, or communicate a decision.
Children: parental consent, or the child's own consent if Gillick competent.
Consent is specific and ongoing — patients can withdraw at any time.
Communication skills: open questions, active listening, no jargon, check understanding (teach-back), non-verbal cues, interpreters when needed.
Record consent and important information given.
examTraps: Assuming a signature equals informed consent.
Using a family member as an interpreter for sensitive information without thought.

diagram.description: Triangle with three corners: voluntary, informed, capacity — 'valid consent' in the centre. Under 'capacity', four boxes: understand, retain, use/weigh, communicate.

goDeeper.heading: Consent for eye drops
goDeeper.body: Before dilating: explain why, the effects (blur, light sensitivity, not driving until vision is clear), rare risks (e.g. angle closure symptoms to watch for), and alternatives. Ask if they have questions, check they agree, and record it. If they decline, record that and the implications you explained.

goDeeper.heading: Teach-back
goDeeper.body: Instead of 'Do you understand?', ask 'Just so I know I've explained it well, can you tell me what you'll do if your eye gets red and painful?' It checks understanding without making the patient feel tested.

goDeeper.heading: Across the UK
goDeeper.body: Capacity law differs between nations (e.g. the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 in Scotland). The principles — presume capacity, support decision-making, act in the person's best interests when they lack capacity — are similar.

flashcards.back: A child with enough understanding and maturity can consent for themselves.
Asking the patient to explain back in their own words to check understanding.

mcq.q: A patient agrees to drops after you say 'I'm just going to put some drops in'. Is this valid consent?

options.text: No: they weren't told the purpose or risks
Yes, because they didn't object to it
Yes, because drops never need consent
Only valid if they sign a consent form
options.feedback: Verbal consent can be valid if it's informed.

mcq.explanation: Patients need to know why, what to expect and the risks before they can give valid consent.

mcq.q: What makes consent valid?

options.text: It's voluntary, informed and with capacity
The patient is over 18 years old

mcq.explanation: Valid consent must be given voluntarily, by someone with capacity, who has been told enough to make an informed choice.

mcq.q: An 80-year-old with mild dementia arrives alone for a sight test. How should you approach consent?

options.text: Assume capacity and assess for this decision
Assume she lacks capacity because of dementia
Refuse to test her until a carer comes
Ask the receptionist to consent for her

mcq.explanation: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, assume capacity unless it's shown otherwise.

original.q: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, you should

mcq.q: A 14-year-old who fully understands a procedure can consent if
mcq.explanation: A child under 16 can consent if they're Gillick competent: they fully understand what's proposed and its implications.

mcq.q: Can a patient withdraw consent part-way through?
mcq.explanation: Consent can be withdrawn at any time, without a reason, and you must stop.

mcq.q: Is implied consent enough for instilling drops?

options.text: Yes, sitting down in the chair implies it

mcq.explanation: Drops are a drug with possible side effects, so they need explicit consent after explaining why and what to expect.

mcq.q: What is 'teach-back'?

options.text: Asking the patient to explain it back to you
Re-reading the record before they leave
Handing over a leaflet to read at home

mcq.explanation: Teach-back means asking the patient to explain the information back in their own words, to check they've understood.

mcq.q: Which is the best opening question in a history?
mcq.explanation: Open with open questions, then use closed ones to clarify.

original.q: Which question type is best to open a history?

mcq.q: What should be recorded about consent?

options.text: That it was given, and what they were told

mcq.explanation: The record should show that consent was given and what the patient was told, so it's clear the consent was informed.

mcq.q: Which is NOT good communication?
mcq.explanation: Jargon can leave patients confused or unable to give informed consent, so explain in plain language.

mcq.q: What is Gillick competence?

options.text: A child under 16 able to consent

mcq.explanation: Gillick competence means a child under 16 has enough understanding and maturity to consent to a particular treatment.

mcq.q: If an adult lacks capacity, decisions are made
mcq.explanation: Under the Mental Capacity Act, decisions for adults who lack capacity must be made in their best interests.

mcq.q: Capacity is

options.text: all or nothing for every decision
linked to age and nothing else

mcq.explanation: Capacity is about a specific decision at a specific time; someone may be able to make some decisions but not others.

mcq.q: The Mental Capacity Act starts by
mcq.explanation: The Mental Capacity Act's first principle is that a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it's shown they lack it.

mcq.q: An unwise decision means

options.text: not, by itself, a lack of capacity
it must be overruled by staff

mcq.explanation: People with capacity can make decisions others think unwise; an unwise choice alone doesn't show lack of capacity.

mcq.q: Who's best for interpreting?

options.text: A neighbour who came with them

mcq.explanation: A professional interpreter is accurate, impartial and bound by confidentiality, unlike family members or neighbours.

mcq.q: Informed consent needs
mcq.explanation: For consent to be informed, the patient needs to know the risks, benefits and alternatives, including doing nothing.

mcq.q: What's active listening?

options.text: Waiting for your turn to talk

mcq.explanation: Active listening means giving full attention, reflecting back what's said and checking you've understood.

mcq.q: SPIKES is a framework for
mcq.explanation: SPIKES (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy) is a framework for breaking bad news.

mcq.q: Non-verbal communication includes

options.text: the words you say and nothing else
what is written in the record

mcq.explanation: Eye contact, posture and tone of voice all affect how a patient feels and how your message comes across.

mcq.q: Which court case set the standard for informing patients about material risks?
mcq.explanation: Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015) set the standard that clinicians must tell patients about any material risks.

mcq.q: Under Montgomery, a risk is 'material' if

options.text: a reasonable patient, or this one, would care
the doctor alone thinks it is significant
it is rare enough to be surprising
it appears on a standard list of risks

mcq.explanation: Under Montgomery, a risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position, or this particular patient, would think it significant.

mcq.q: A patient understands the risks of dilation and can repeat them back, but can't weigh them up to decide. What does the Mental Capacity Act say?

options.text: They may lack capacity, as weighing up is part of the test
They have capacity, because they understood the risks
Capacity is never assessed for eye drops
The family automatically decides for them

mcq.explanation: The test asks whether the person can understand, retain, weigh up and communicate the decision.

original.q: The Mental Capacity Act test asks whether the person can

options.text: understand, retain, weigh up and communicate the decision

mcq.q: A lasting power of attorney for health and welfare allows

options.text: a chosen person to decide if capacity is lost
anyone close to the patient to decide
the optometrist to decide on their behalf

mcq.explanation: A health and welfare lasting power of attorney lets a person chosen in advance make health decisions if the patient loses capacity.

mcq.q: An IMCA is

options.text: an independent advocate for people who lack capacity
an interpreter for patients who don't speak English
a solicitor who handles the patient's affairs
a family member chosen to speak for the patient

mcq.explanation: An Independent Mental Capacity Advocate (IMCA) speaks for people who lack capacity and have no one else to represent them.

mcq.q: 16- and 17-year-olds in England are

options.text: presumed to have capacity to consent
never able to consent for themselves
always needing a parent to consent
treated the same as children under 12

mcq.explanation: In England, 16- and 17-year-olds are presumed to have capacity to consent to their own treatment.

mcq.q: Implied consent is shown when a patient

options.text: rests their chin on the slit lamp
says nothing at all when you start
refuses when you describe the test
gets up and leaves the room

mcq.explanation: Resting their chin on the slit lamp shows by action that the patient agrees to be examined: implied consent.

mcq.q: What does ICE stand for in consultations?
mcq.explanation: ICE stands for Ideas, Concerns and Expectations: what the patient thinks is going on, what worries them and what they hope for.

mcq.q: Which consultation model is widely used in UK healthcare teaching?
mcq.explanation: The Calgary-Cambridge model is widely used to teach consultation skills in UK healthcare.

mcq.q: How should you speak to a patient who lip-reads?

options.text: Face them, in good light, and speak clearly
Shout so that they can hear you
Turn away while you write notes
Cover your mouth while you speak

mcq.explanation: Lip-readers need to see your face clearly, so face them in good light and speak clearly at a normal pace.

mcq.q: How should you guide a patient with sight loss?

options.text: Offer your arm and describe the way
Pull them along by the hand
Leave them to find their own way

mcq.explanation: Offer your arm so they can hold it just above the elbow and walk half a step behind, and describe steps and obstacles.

mcq.q: Which material helps patients with learning disabilities?
mcq.explanation: Easy-read information uses short sentences and pictures, which many people with learning disabilities find easier.

mcq.q: A patient is angry about waiting. What's a good first response?

options.text: Argue that the wait was unavoidable
Ignore it and start the test
Ask them to leave the practice

mcq.explanation: Acknowledging the patient's frustration and apologising usually calms things down better than arguing.

mcq.q: Why avoid jargon?
mcq.explanation: Patients may not understand jargon, which can leave them confused or unable to make informed decisions.

mcq.q: A reflective statement such as 'It sounds like you're worried about your sight' shows
mcq.explanation: Naming the patient's feelings shows you've noticed and understood them, which is empathy.

mcq.q: Why summarise at the end of the consultation?

options.text: To check understanding and agree the plan
To fill time at the end
It's not needed if they nodded
So the practice can bill for it

mcq.explanation: Summarising checks the patient has understood and confirms the agreed plan before they leave.

mcq.q: Which is the best way to give complex information?

options.text: In small chunks, checking as you go
All at once, so nothing is missed
In writing only, with no talking
Not at all, to avoid worrying them

mcq.explanation: Giving complex information in small chunks and checking understanding as you go helps patients take it in.

mcq.q: Patients with dementia may need

options.text: simple language, more time and carers involved
faster explanations to hold their attention
no explanation, as they won't remember
to be left out of decisions altogether

mcq.explanation: People with dementia often need simple language, more time and their carers involved, while still being included in decisions.

mcq.q: Consent for clinical photographs used in teaching should be
mcq.explanation: Photos used for teaching need specific, recorded consent because they go beyond the patient's direct care.

mcq.q: Who has parental responsibility?

options.text: Usually the birth mother, often the father
Any adult who brings the child

mcq.explanation: The birth mother automatically has parental responsibility, and the father usually does if married to the mother or named on the birth certificate.

mcq.q: A competent adult refuses dilation. What should you do?

options.text: Respect it, explain the risks and record it
Dilate anyway, as it's in their interest
Refuse to continue with any of the test
Accept it but leave it out of the notes

mcq.explanation: A competent adult can refuse any test. Respect it, explain the risks of not doing it and record the refusal.

mcq.q: What's the danger of 'yes' questions with anxious patients?

options.text: They may agree to avoid seeming difficult

cases.scenario: A patient who has never had drops before is about to be dilated. They drove to the appointment alone.
cases.question: What must you cover to get valid consent?
cases.modelAnswer: Consent must be voluntary, informed and given by someone with capacity. Explain in plain language why dilation is recommended, what it involves, and the effects: blurred vision, especially for near, and light sensitivity for several hours, so they should not drive until their vision has cleared. Mention the small risk of raised eye pressure and the symptoms to report. Offer alternatives, such as rebooking with someone to drive them, check understanding, and invite questions. Respect their decision, and record the discussion and the consent given.

topics.title: Interprofessional learning (IPL)
topics.summary: Interprofessional learning brings students from different health professions together to learn with, from and about each other, so they can work better as teams and improve patient care. Your IPL session is compulsory.
keyPoints: Definition (CAIPE): when two or more professions learn with, from and about each other to improve collaboration and the quality of care.
Your IPL session: Thu 19 Nov, 14:00–16:00 (rooms G77/79/81) — compulsory.
Know other eye-care roles: dispensing opticians, orthoptists, ophthalmologists, ophthalmic nurses, GPs, pharmacists.
Optometrists often refer to and work alongside GPs, pharmacists and hospital eye services.
Clear communication between professions (e.g. SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) reduces errors.
Respect for each profession's expertise and scope is central to good teamwork.
Reflect on what you learned about other roles and how it changes your practice.
examTraps: Treating IPL as just 'meeting other students' rather than learning about roles and teamwork.

Pharmacists advise on medicines, including eye drops and side effects.

cases.scenario: A care home resident with dementia and diabetes has fallen twice this month. You find dense cataracts and badly scratched spectacles.
cases.question: Who else needs to be involved?
cases.modelAnswer: Good care here is shared. Refer for cataract assessment with a clear account of the functional impact and the falls. Tell the GP, who oversees diabetes, medication and the falls assessment. Involve the care home staff, who can keep spectacles clean, labelled and worn. A falls or physiotherapy team, an occupational therapist for lighting and contrast at home, and the diabetic eye screening service all have a role. Involve the family, or whoever holds lasting power of attorney, in decisions if the resident lacks capacity. Record who you contacted and what was agreed.

topics.title: Reflective practice
topics.summary: From the week 3 PPD lecture: reflection turns experience into learning. The GOC expects critical reflection throughout your career, so know the models, what good academic reflective writing looks like, and how to write a CPD reflection.
keyPoints: GOC definition (CPD guide, 2024): thinking analytically about your experiences to gain insight and improve the way you work and the care you give. Linked to GOC outcomes 7.4 and 5.1.
Critical reflection moves from describing to analysing: evaluate current practice, consider what's desirable and what's possible, and form new understanding that changes what you do.
Models: Driscoll (2000) / Rolfe et al. (2001), 'What? So what? Now what?', and Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988): description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.

Academic reflective writing isn't just description, a diary, self-disclosure, flattery of the course or uncritical referencing. It needs structure, formal language and evidence of learning and how you'll use it.
Benefits: embeds good practice, improves quality of care and assures the public.
CPD reflections: what you expected, what you learned, and whether and how you'll apply it. Anonymise: nothing that identifies a patient or practitioner.
Prompt questions: what happened, key takeaways, how issues were addressed, what you'd do differently, the impact, quick changes and longer-term gaps.
examTraps: Writing a reflection that only describes what happened.
Including details that could identify a patient or colleague.

diagram.description: Circular diagram with six stages and arrows: Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusion, Action plan, returning to Description.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: other models
goDeeper.body: Kolb's cycle (experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation) and Schön's reflection-in-action (during) versus reflection-on-action (after). flashcards.back: Description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.
In-action = during the event; on-action = afterwards (Schön).

cases.scenario: During an assessed routine you forget to check pupils. Your supervisor points it out afterwards.
cases.question: Write a brief structured reflection.
cases.modelAnswer: Describe what happened: I omitted pupil testing in a timed routine. Feelings: embarrassed, and worried about what I might have missed. Evaluation: the rest went well, but I rushed after falling behind in history taking. Analysis: I have no fixed order for the preliminary tests, so under pressure a step dropped out, and a relative afferent pupillary defect could have gone unnoticed. Conclusion: a consistent sequence matters more than speed. Action plan: write and rehearse a fixed order, practise it timed with a partner three times this week, and ask my supervisor to observe again.
